prompt.context: Bob is a master brewer and has been brewing beer for the past decade. Upon graduating from Stern, he opened a brewery on the Upper West Side called Something Witty that features Belgian Witbier styled brews. While he found early success, he has noticed an increase in customers asking for gluten-free alternatives, such as cider. Bob has hired us to help him analyze his options.
prompt.question: How should Bob evaluate his options for responding to growing customer demand for gluten-free alternatives like cider?

clarifying_info.a: Bob's goal is to continue to be profitable regardless of what expansion opportunity he explores.

clarifying_info.q: What does Bob currently sell and how?
clarifying_info.a: Currently, Bob only sells bottled beer direct to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: How many bottles are in a case?
How many days does production run?
clarifying_info.a: Production runs Monday through Friday (assume 20 days per month).

exhibits.title: Bottled Beverage Production
exhibits.shows: A table comparing beer and cider production capacity and selling prices under two scenarios: Current State and After Renovations for Cider Production.

framework: Alternatives: other drinks (wine, cocktails, cider), experiences (live music, themed nights), food
Costs: renovations, equipment, licensing, break-even point
Market: size, competitors, customer tastes/preferences, cannibalization
Capabilities: organic production (equipment, training, ingredients, sufficient space) vs. outsource/purchase from another manufacturer; current capacity utilization

questions.prompt: Question 1a: Bob has decided to explore expansion into cider. Based on Exhibit 1, what are your thoughts on the two production options (Current State vs. After Renovations)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize: (1) Current State pros: specialization in one product, one clear consistent marketing message, specialized labor force. Current State cons: not meeting demand for gluten-free customers, not increasing revenue potential. (2) After Renovations pros: new product offering, cider has a higher selling price than beer. After Renovations cons: beer production decreases by 6 cases/day, costs of renovation. Candidate should also flag that there are other ways to expand into cider beyond renovating the factory (e.g., building a new factory, buying cider from an existing company and reselling).

questions.prompt: Question 1b: What will be the change in Bob's annual revenue if he begins to produce cider?
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up a before-and-after revenue comparison. Key data to provide if asked: 30 bottles per case; production Monday-Friday (20 days/month). Revenues would increase by $302,400 annually. A strong candidate may also simplify by calculating only the change in revenue (lost beer revenue + gained cider revenue).

math.setup: Compare annual revenue after renovations vs. current annual revenue. 20 days/month x 12 months = 240 production days/year. Current beer revenue = 30 cases/day x 30 bottles/case x $5.00 x 240 days. Post-renovation beer revenue = 24 cases/day x 30 bottles/case x $5.00 x 240 days. New cider revenue = 12 cases/day x 30 bottles/case x $6.00 x 240 days.
steps: Current annual beer revenue: 30 x 30 x $5.00 x 240 = $1,080,000
Post-renovation beer revenue: 24 x 30 x $5.00 x 240 = $864,000
New cider revenue: 12 x 30 x $6.00 x 240 = $518,400

questions.prompt: Question 2: Besides potential revenue, what other factors should Bob consider before expanding into the cider market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should quickly identify cost as a key factor, then brainstorm other ideas across: Cost (labor training, equipment, labeling, marketing, raw materials such as apples), Market Size/Demand (cider vs. beer market size, number of new customers, expected future demand, growth rates of both markets), Go-to-Market Strategy, Impact to Core (cannibalization, brand equity), New Distribution Channels (grocery, liquor stores).

questions.prompt: Question 3: Bob has determined that he needs to capture at least 0.5% of the NYC take-home cider market annually to break even. Will he be able to produce enough cider to capture 0.5%?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use cider production volume calculated in Question 1b (86,400 bottles/year) and compare it to 0.5% of NYC cider market. NYC cider market = 15.5 million bottles expected to be sold next year. 0.5% of market = 77,500 bottles. Since 86,400 > 77,500, Bob can produce enough. A bonus insight: demand for Bob's cider has not been confirmed — he can produce enough to break even, but can he actually sell that amount?

math.setup: Calculate Bob's annual cider production, then compare to 0.5% of NYC market size.
steps: Bob's annual cider production: 12 cases/day x 30 bottles/case x 240 days = 86,400 bottles/year
86,400 > 77,500, so Bob can produce enough to capture the required market share.
math.answer: Yes, Bob can produce 86,400 bottles/year, which exceeds the 77,500-bottle break-even threshold (0.5% of 15.5M bottles).

brainstorming.prompt: Besides potential revenue, what other factors should Bob consider before expanding into the cider market?

categories.name: Market Size and Demand
ideas: Relative size of cider vs. beer market in NYC
Number of new customers cider could attract
Growth rates of both the cider and craft beer markets

categories.name: Go-to-Market Strategy
ideas: How to introduce cider alongside existing beer brand

categories.name: Impact to Core Business
ideas: Effect on brand equity and identity as a beer brewery

recommendation: Bob should make the investment to produce cider. He will see an increase in revenues of $302,400 per year and should be able to break even based on his 0.5% market capture calculation (he can produce 86,400 bottles vs. the 77,500-bottle threshold).
risks: Demand risk: while Bob can produce enough to break even, it is not confirmed he can sell that amount in practice
next_steps: Conduct competitive analysis of the NYC cider market
Pressure test Bob's assumptions about achieving 0.5% market capture
Conduct market research to determine optimal price point, flavor, and packaging
Assess what is happening to the cider market going forward and whether Bob can meet demand
Quantify renovation and equipment costs to validate the break-even assumption
